To detain someone means to hold them and prevent them from leaving. The person being detained cannot walk away freely — they are being kept in place by someone with authority or power over them.

Think of it this way: if you are detained, your movement and freedom are under someone else's control, at least for a period of time.

Detain is used in two related but slightly different situations:

1. The Primary Sense — Official or Legal Holding

This is the most important and widely used meaning. Here, a person (usually a police officer, soldier, border official, immigration authority, or some other figure of authority) physically holds someone and does not allow them to leave — often for the purpose of questioning, investigation, or security.

  • The police detained the man for questioning after the robbery.
  • Soldiers detained several civilians at the checkpoint.
  • Airport security detained a passenger whose documents did not match.
  • The government detained the journalist for writing against the regime.

Notice the key features here:

  • The person being detained has not chosen to stay — they are being held.
  • There is usually a reason: investigation, suspicion, security risk, legal process.
  • It is typically temporary, though it can sometimes last days, months, or even years in extreme cases.
  • The person detained has restricted freedom — they may be kept in a room, a cell, a facility, or simply told they cannot leave.

2. The Secondary Sense — Keeping Someone's Time

In a gentler, more polite or formal context, detain can simply mean to hold someone up or delay them — to take up their time and prevent them from going where they need to go. No force or authority is involved here; it is just the idea of keeping someone occupied.

  • "I won't detain you any longer — I know you're busy." (Meaning: I won't keep holding up your time.)
  • The long meeting detained the employees well past 6 o'clock.
  • A phone call detained her, so she arrived late.

This second sense is more formal and old-fashioned in feel. You are more likely to encounter it in writing, formal speech, or polite conversation. In everyday speech, people usually just say "keep" or "hold up" in these situations.
What Makes "Detain" Different from Similar Words

Understanding a word deeply means knowing how it differs from words that seem similar. Here are the key distinctions:

Detain vs. Arrest

These two are often confused, but they are not the same.

  • To arrest someone means to formally take them into custody because you believe they have committed a crime. An arrest usually comes with formal charges or the clear intention to charge.
  • To detain someone is less formal and more preliminary. You can be detained without being arrested — meaning you are being held and cannot leave, but you haven't officially been charged with anything yet. Detention often comes before arrest, while authorities investigate or gather more information.

Example: The police detained the man for three hours before deciding there was enough evidence to formally arrest him.

Detain vs. Imprison / Jail

  • To imprison or jail someone means to lock them away as a result of being found guilty — it is the result of a legal process.
  • To detain someone is usually earlier in the process — no conviction is required, and it can happen without any formal legal proceedings.

You can be detained and later released without ever being jailed.

Detain vs. Hold / Keep

  • Hold and keep are everyday, neutral words meaning much the same thing.
  • Detain is more formal and carries a stronger sense of authority and restriction of freedom. It also specifically implies the person does not want to stay — they are being kept against their will or free choice.

If someone says "the police held him," it feels casual. If they say "the police detained him," it feels official, serious, and precise.
The Feeling and Weight of the Word

Detain carries a serious tone. It suggests a power imbalance — someone with authority is holding someone who does not have the power to simply walk away. Even in the gentler second sense (keeping someone's time), there is a formal quality to the word.

In news reports and journalism, you will frequently see this word used when covering conflicts, law enforcement, immigration, or political situations:

  • "Human rights groups reported that dozens of protesters were detained overnight."
  • "The suspect was detained pending further investigation."
  • "Refugees were detained at the border for weeks without explanation."

When you see detain used in these contexts, it often signals that the people involved may not have been formally charged, that their legal status is uncertain, or that their freedom has been suspended without a full legal process — which is why human rights organizations pay close attention to detention.

Typically: police, military, border officials, immigration authorities, security personnel, governments, or any body with legal or institutional power.

However, in the softer sense, even a long-winded professor can "detain" students after class simply by keeping them from leaving on time.

When someone has been detained, that person is called a detainee. The act of being held is called detention. A place where people are held — especially in an immigration or legal context — is called a detention center or detention facility.

Detain is a formal word. You would naturally use it in:

  • Legal or official documents
  • News articles and journalism
  • Academic writing
  • Formal speech

In casual, everyday conversation, you would more likely say:

  • "The cops held him."
  • "She kept me waiting."
  • "They stopped us at the border."

But if you want to sound precise and formal — especially in writing — detain is exactly the right word.

AspectDetail

Detain means to hold someone and prevent them from leaving. In its most important sense, it refers to official or legal holding of a person — by police, military, or other authorities — for purposes like questioning or investigation, without necessarily charging them with a crime. In a softer sense, it can mean to hold up or take up someone's time. It is a formal, serious word that implies restriction of freedom, a power imbalance, and the unwillingness of the detained person to stay. It is less formal than imprison (which follows conviction) and less formal than arrest (which involves charges), but more serious and official-sounding than everyday words like hold or keep.
